rationale.complete: Round 1 done: dated predictions, synthetic validation on real call grids (32 runs), 71 units in 35 goal periods with day-blocked CV, shift and day-block nulls and t_call sensitivity, four native tests (NE41, NE14, G51, G19), a post-hoc named-message test, and confirm.py (C1-C5) dry-run on stand-ins. Holdout not run; two-layer call-process model not built.
rationale.faithfulness: The core claim (a read-out kernel raises n_cross and makes it consistent) is refuted in the coherent comparison: n_cross falls from 0.061 (exponential) to 0.004 once the recipient's call clock is modelled, and it is regime-dependent. The pre-registered wins are void (synthetic guard failed). Only the hop-1 shape and the regime-I native survive. Scorecard A1 B1 C1 D0 E0 F1 G1 H0 I0.
rationale.usefulness: A diagnostic with teeth for anyone fitting influence or branching models to agent logs: model each agent's call clock and call class first, or timestamps measure the scaffold, and shift nulls will not catch it. Plus a post-hoc operator handle (naming an agent raises its talk at the next call, about 0.15 per message in the always-on regime) that restates H29's naming lever. Not a new control knob.

one_line: Anchoring cross-excitation at the recipient's next call removes most of H03's apparent triggering: talk timing follows each agent's own call clock, and only messages that name the recipient (regime III, post hoc) excite it.

v2.claim: Talk timing follows each agent's call clock; cross-triggering ≈ 0 except named messages
v2.decision: model agents on their own clocks
v2.rater: coordinator first pass (from integrated reports); independent rater pending
